title: Range Sum of BST
description: Brute force to optimized: visiting every node versus pruning entire subtrees using BST ordering.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given the root of a binary search tree and two integers low and high, return the sum of values of all nodes with a value in the inclusive range [low, high].

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","root (a BST), low, high"],["Output","The sum of all node values in [low, high]"],["Goal","Prune entire subtrees using the BST property, avoiding visiting every node"],["Constraints","Up to 2*10^4 nodes"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Sum values within a range, in a BST\"","Use the BST ordering to prune entire subtrees that cannot possibly contain a value in range"],["A value outside the range on one side","The corresponding subtree can be skipped entirely, not just that one node"]]}

blocks.text: If a node's value is less than low, every value in its LEFT subtree is even smaller (by the BST property), so the entire left subtree can be skipped; only the right subtree might still contain valid values. Symmetrically, if a node's value exceeds high, its entire right subtree can be skipped.

blocks.title: Analogy: Summing Filed Documents Within a Number Range, Skipping Irrelevant Drawers
blocks.text: Picture a filing cabinet sorted by number, and wanting to sum all documents within a range. If a drawer's entire contents are known to be below your range, you can skip that whole drawer (and everything filed even lower) without checking each document individually.

blocks.caption: A node outside [low,high] lets you skip an entire subtree, not just that node

blocks.text: Result: 32. Nodes 10, 7, 15 fall within [7,15], summing to 32.

Before visiting every node and checking each individually, notice that the BST property lets an out-of-range node prune an ENTIRE subtree, not just itself, since everything in that subtree is guaranteed to also be out of range.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If node.val < low, everything in its left subtree is even smaller (still < low), so only the right subtree needs checking.

Observation 2: If node.val > high, everything in its right subtree is even larger (still > high), so only the left subtree needs checking.

Observation 3: If node.val falls within [low, high], include it in the sum, and recurse into BOTH subtrees, since either could still contain valid values.

Observation 4: This recursive pruning avoids descending into subtrees that provably cannot contribute to the answer.
This leads to a recursive traversal that prunes: skip the left subtree if the current value is below low, skip the right if above high, otherwise include the value and recurse both ways.
Traverse every node in the tree (any standard traversal), adding its value to the sum if it falls within [low, high].
Why the code is written this way

items: Visiting every node directly and checking each is correct regardless of tree structure.
It never prunes based on the BST property, costing O(n) even when the range is very restrictive.

blocks.text: Limitation: pruning entire subtrees using the BST property can skip large portions of the tree, especially for narrow ranges.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Instead of visiting every node, check at each node whether its value already disqualifies an entire subtree (too small skips the left, too large skips the right), only recursing into subtrees that could still contain valid values.
At each node: if val < low, recurse only right; if val > high, recurse only left; otherwise, add val and recurse both directions.
Dry run for root = [10,5,15,3,7,null,18], low=7, high=15

blocks.content: {"headers":["Node","Action"],"rows":[["10","in range, add 10, recurse both"],["5","5<7, skip left (3), recurse right (7)"],["7","in range, add 7"],["15","in range, add 15, recurse both"],["18","18>15, skip right, recurse left (none)"]]}

blocks.text: The BST property guarantees that if a node's value is already too small, everything in its left subtree is even smaller, so it can never contribute to the sum; the symmetric argument holds for values too large and the right subtree. Pruning these subtrees entirely, rather than visiting and rejecting each node individually, can save significant work for narrow ranges.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) worst case, but often much less due to pruning; O(height + matches) is a tighter bound in practice.
Space: O(height) recursion depth.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Visit every node","O(n) always","O(height)","Correct, but never exploits the BST property."],["Prune subtrees using BST ordering","O(n) worst case, often much less","O(height)","The expected, efficient solution."]]}

blocks.text: Range Sum of BST demonstrates pruning entire subtrees (not just individual nodes) using the BST property, a technique broadly applicable to range queries on BSTs.

items: Still recursing into both subtrees even when the BST property proves one is entirely out of range, wasting the pruning opportunity.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["low equals high","Sums just that single value if present, 0 otherwise."],["The range covers the entire tree's value span","Sums every node, equivalent to the brute force."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "an out-of-range node prunes an entire subtree, not just itself" is the key insight to state clearly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "sum/count values in a range, in a BST", think: prune entire subtrees using the BST ordering.

Trim a Binary Search Tree, using the identical subtree-pruning technique for a different goal.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both approaches share the same worst-case bound, but pruning can save substantial work for narrow ranges in practice.

items: Pattern: prune entire subtrees using BST ordering, rather than visiting every node.
Core Idea: skip the left subtree if too small, the right if too large, otherwise include the value and recurse both ways.
Time: O(n) always for the brute force, O(n) worst case but often less for the pruned approach.
Most Important Observation: an out-of-range value prunes its entire corresponding subtree, not just itself.
Interview Difficulty: an accessible BST range-query problem.
One line memory trick: too small skips left, too large skips right, otherwise include and recurse both.
